Reciprocal-Tail Rigidity: Theorems, Proofs and Questions

Erdős #243 48 pp Equations typeset from the exact TeX

Précis

A claim-bounded complete reasoning record for Erdős #243. It retains the centred-state dynamics, negative-mass recovery, bounded-rise and periodic exclusions, conditional bounded-negative result, residue mechanisms, and all registered families. Mixed-sign unbounded negative excursions remain uncontrolled, so the original eventual-recurrence problem remains open.

This paper owns the complete problem-specific reasoning surface for Erdős #243, including all registered result families and their boundaries.

It is not authority for the validity of claims tagged Lean, which belongs to the cited kernel-checked source, or a solution to Erdős #243, which remains open.

Introduction

Throughout, 𝑧+ =max(𝑧,0)z+=max(z,0). Statements about a tail permit deletion of a finite prefix, but the index in a specified higher-order rate is retained. In particular, 1 +3/𝑛 +𝑜(𝑛−3)1+3/n+o(n−3) must not be silently replaced by the same formula in a shifted index. Positive integer hypotheses refer to ordinary integers, not merely positive real states.

Sylvester’s sequence 2,3,7,43,1807,…2,3,7,43,1807,… is generated by 𝑎𝑛 =𝑎2𝑛−1 −𝑎𝑛−1 +1an=an−12−an−1+1 and has reciprocal sum 11; the recurrence is equivalent to the telescoping identity

1𝑎𝑛−1−1=1𝑎𝑛−1+1𝑎𝑛−1.1an−1−1=1an−1+1an−1.

Consequently the tail beginning with 1/𝑎𝑛−11/an−1 equals 1/(𝑎𝑛−1 −1)1/(an−1−1). Erdős Problem #243 asserts that this is the only way a sequence of that growth can have a rational reciprocal sum:

Problem 1.1 (Erdős #243). Let 1 ≤𝑎1 <𝑎2 <⋯1≤a1<a2<⋯ be a sequence of integers with

lim𝑛→∞𝑎𝑛𝑎2𝑛−1=1and∑1𝑎𝑛∈ℚ.limn→∞anan−12=1and∑1an∈Q.

Then 𝑎𝑛 =𝑎2𝑛−1 −𝑎𝑛−1 +1an=an−12−an−1+1 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n.

See [5] and [6]. The supplied catalogue snapshot labels it open [13]; no fresh catalogue-status verification is claimed for this revision. Below we index the same recurrence as 𝑎𝑛+1 =𝑎2𝑛 −𝑎𝑛 +1an+1=an2−an+1, which is the shift the formal sources use; the two forms are the same statement. Write syl⁡(𝑎) =𝑎2 −𝑎 +1syl⁡(a)=a2−a+1, the Sylvester successor.

The hypothesis is asymptotic and the conclusion is exact. Clearing a rational tail as 𝐶𝑛/𝐷𝑛Cn/Dn exposes that distinction in the integer 𝐸𝑛 =𝐷𝑛 −(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛En=Dn−(an−1)Cn: a Sylvester tail has 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0, while quadratic growth only gives 𝐸𝑛/𝐶𝑛 →0En/Cn→0. Integrality alone cannot turn this relative estimate into 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 when 𝐶𝑛Cn grows. The exact dynamics retain extra information: old divisors persist, and they constrain which numerator heights the orbit can visit. This is the arithmetic information used by the bounded-negative and record-crossing arguments.

Section 2 carries out that conversion at one prescribed rate and settles the assertion of Problem 1.1 on the resulting class of sequences. Section 3 places the theorem against the published sufficient conditions, states the evidence class of every result here, and guides the rest of the note.

Keywords. irrationality; Ahmes series; Sylvester’s sequence; unit fractions; Lean 4. MSC 2020. 11J72 (primary); 11B37, 11D68, 68V20 (secondary).

Irrationality at the cubic rate

The short note treats the cubic-rate theorem as a further consequence. This section supplies its full polynomial and number-field argument. The canonical integer state is constructed first; the general error coordinates are developed in Section 4.

Theorem 2.1 (cubic-rate irrationality). If strictly increasing positive integers satisfy 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 =1 +3/𝑛 +𝑜(𝑛−3)an2/an+1=1+3/n+o(n−3), then ∑𝑛1/𝑎𝑛∑n1/an is irrational.

Theorem 2.2 (rising-factorial cubic exclusion). Let 𝑎,𝐶,𝐷 :ℕ →ℤ>0a,C,D:N→Z>0 satisfy

𝐶𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝐶𝑛−𝐷𝑛,𝐷𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛.(1)(1)Cn+1=anCn−Dn,Dn+1=anDn.

Then for every 𝐴 ∈ℚ>0A∈Q>0 and every 𝐵 ∈ℚB∈Q,

lim inf𝑋→∞#{𝑛≤𝑋:𝐶𝑛≠𝐴𝑛(𝑛+1)(𝑛+2)+𝐵}𝑋>0.lim infX→∞#{n≤X:Cn≠An(n+1)(n+2)+B}X>0.

In particular no such orbit satisfies 𝐶𝑛 =𝐴 𝑛(𝑛 +1)(𝑛 +2) +𝐵Cn=An(n+1)(n+2)+B for all large 𝑛n.

The irrationality theorem needs only exclusion of eventual equality. Theorem 2.2 proves more: the exceptional set has strictly positive lower density. Equivalently, no subsequence of prefix lengths can have an exceptional proportion tending to zero. The density constant may depend on the orbit and on the proposed cubic. The two restrictions that meet on the same cubic are integrality, which supplies the rising-factorial shape and the scale, and the denominator transport, which imposes an arithmetic square condition; the scale calculation and the two residue words that close the argument can be checked on the page.

This is an ordinary proof. The finite claims include the two words (14) and (15), the image {0,2,5,6}{0,2,5,6} modulo 77, the divisor condition (𝑟2 +𝑠2)2 ∣48(r2+s2)2∣48, and the scalar sequence 𝑛(𝑛 +1)(𝑛 +2) +( −1)𝑛n(n+1)(n+2)+(−1)n. The public checkpoint also contains formalised polynomial extraction, primitive cubic normalisation and finite transport results, including the primitive-shape theorem. These are components, not an assembled proof of Theorem 2.1. No declaration of that complete irrationality implication has been identified in the supplied source index. Lemma 2.6 uses the classical finite-Galois Chebotarev theorem; its use must be justified by the number-field argument, not by finite residue computations.

Position.

Theorem 2.1 carries no rationality hypothesis and no state hypothesis, and it is the principal irrationality theorem proved in this record. Its rate class lies inside the growth hypothesis of Problem 1.1, because 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 =1 +3/𝑛 +𝑜(𝑛−3)an2/an+1=1+3/n+o(n−3) forces 𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛 →1an+1/an2→1. On that class the assertion of Problem 1.1 therefore holds, by exclusion of a rational reciprocal sum, and the recurrence is never exhibited; Sylvester’s own sequence, whose ratio 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1an2/an+1 is 1 +𝑂(1/𝑎𝑛)1+O(1/an), lies outside the class. The rate 1 +3/𝑛1+3/n sits beyond the hypotheses recorded in Section 3. The product weight 𝑃𝑛/𝑎𝑛Pn/an grows like 𝑛3n3 at this rate, so (𝑃𝑛/𝑎𝑛)(𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 −1)(Pn/an)(an2/an+1−1) tends to infinity and Koizumi’s Corollary 4(1) does not apply; the rate also fails his 1 +𝑜(1/𝑛)1+o(1/n) condition, and ∑𝑛𝛾𝑛∑nγn diverges, so Duverney’s convergent-defect hypothesis does not apply. Whether the LCM-weighted criteria apply on this class is not decided here, since the ratio of the two weights is the overlap factor. Theorem 2.2 uses positive integer 𝑎𝑛,𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛an,Cn,Dn and the exact recurrences (1), but does not require near-quadratic growth. The later sufficient criteria are not asserted to subsume the cubic-rate argument.

The display defining the canonical integer tail gives 𝐶𝑛 =𝑞(∏𝑘<𝑛𝑎𝑘 ⋅∑𝑚1/𝑎𝑚 −∑𝑘<𝑛∏𝑗<𝑛,𝑗≠𝑘𝑎𝑗)Cn=q(∏k<nak⋅∑m1/am−∑k<n∏j<n,j≠kaj), a linear form in the reciprocal sum with integer coefficients. Approximation criteria for irrationality use nonzero forms of this kind that tend to zero. At the cubic rate the integers 𝐶𝑛Cn grow: Lemma 2.11 gives 𝐶𝑛+1/𝐶𝑛 =1 +3/𝑛 +𝑜(𝑛−3)Cn+1/Cn=1+3/n+o(n−3), so 𝐶𝑛Cn is a positive multiple of 𝑛(𝑛 +1)(𝑛 +2)n(n+1)(n+2) up to a factor tending to one. The proof above uses this rate at precision 𝑜(𝑛−3)o(n−3): Lemma 2.10 turns it into the exact profile 𝐶𝑛 =𝐴 𝑛(𝑛 +1)(𝑛 +2) +𝐵Cn=An(n+1)(n+2)+B, which Theorem 2.2 excludes.

Prior work, and the status of the note

Classical sufficient conditions and the pseudo-greedy formulation.

The rational-tail method predates these coordinates. Erdős and Straus [15] use eventual integer remainders under a small-numerator hypothesis. For polynomial Cantor series, Hančl and Tijdeman decompose the numerator into finitely many shifted products; rationality is characterised by the vanishing of the resulting polynomial sum [16]. We use that polynomial theorem as methodological context, not as an unrestricted theorem about arrays of signed integer coefficients. The finite-to-infinite rearrangement requires boundary control, which is available in the polynomial setting. Neither cited result supplies the bounded-negative first-crossing argument proved below.

Several classical results give sufficient conditions directly on the sequence (𝑎𝑛)(an). Their precise hypotheses must be compared separately with the bounded-defect, summability and prescribed-rate conditions here. Duverney imposes a different sufficient analytic hypothesis; the Erdős–Straus one, read through the dictionary of the next paragraph, is implied by nonnegativity of 𝐸E, the hypothesis of Theorem 8.1, so that criterion already covers the descent of Section 8 (see ). Erdős and Straus proved that if lim𝑎𝑛/𝑎2𝑛−1 =1liman/an−12=1, the reciprocal sum is rational, and 𝑎𝑛an does not satisfy the recurrence, then

lim sup𝑛→∞ [𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛]𝑎𝑛+1(𝑎2𝑛+1𝑎𝑛+2−1)>0,lim supn→∞ [a1,…,an]an+1(an+12an+2−1)>0,

where [𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛][a1,…,an] is the least common multiple [1]. This is the indexing in the original theorem. Erdős’s 1988 survey, followed by the supplied catalogue summary, instead prints 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 −1an2/an+1−1 in the second factor while retaining the same prefix-LCM quotient; that displayed summary is off by one and is not followed here [6][13]. Koizumi records the convenient sufficient rate 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 =1 +𝑜(1/𝑛)an2/an+1=1+o(1/n) under which the Erdős–Straus criterion settles the problem [12]. Tijdeman and Yuan give a criterion of the same kind for Ahmes series with positive integer numerators, weighted by the least common multiple of the earlier denominators .

Duverney proved a conditional signed form of the problem itself: for signs 𝜖𝑛 ∈{ −1,1}ϵn∈{−1,1}, if ∑𝑛≥0(𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛 −1)∑n≥0(an+1/an2−1) converges, then the reciprocal sum with numerators 𝜖𝑛ϵn is rational if and only if

𝑎𝑛+1=𝑎2𝑛−(𝜖𝑛+1/𝜖𝑛)𝑎𝑛+𝜖𝑛+2/𝜖𝑛+1an+1=an2−(ϵn+1/ϵn)an+ϵn+2/ϵn+1

for all large 𝑛n [2]. Absolute convergence is a stronger sufficient specialisation, not the hypothesis printed in that corollary. The all-positive specialisation is the form relevant here.

A different quantitative question is treated by Duverney, Kurosawa and Shiokawa [17]. For rational 𝑥𝑛 >1xn>1, their result assumes eventual 𝑥𝑛+1 ≥𝑥2𝑛xn+1≥xn2 and control of the accumulated denominators of 𝑥𝑛+1/𝑥2𝑛xn+1/xn2; it computes the irrationality exponent of a signed reciprocal series. We use it only as a restricted comparison. In particular, a Sylvester tail and the cubic rate considered here approach quadratic growth from the other side.

Badea’s positive-term criterion is adjacent but different: for positive rational terms 𝑏𝑛/𝑎𝑛bn/an, eventual strict inequality

𝑎𝑛+1>𝑏𝑛+1𝑏𝑛𝑎2𝑛−𝑏𝑛+1𝑏𝑛𝑎𝑛+1an+1>bn+1bnan2−bn+1bnan+1

forces irrationality, while rationality under the corresponding non-strict inequality forces eventual equality [3]. For 𝑏𝑛 =1bn=1, the non-strict inequality is compatible with the familiar nonnegative-error descent after passage to the rational tail. It does not cover arbitrary signed centred errors. The general positive-coefficient criterion is not identified as a checked theorem in the supplied evidence.

Koizumi’s work on doubly exponential sequences [12] bears directly on the state system used below, and supplies the coordinates in which several of the statements of this note are most naturally read. For a rational 𝑟 =𝑝/𝑞r=p/q with pseudo-greedy expansion (𝑎𝑛)(an), remainders (𝑥𝑛)(xn) and gap sequence 𝜀𝑛 =𝑥−1𝑛 +1 −𝑎𝑛εn=xn−1+1−an, his Lemma 4  [12] produces integers 𝑐𝑛 >0cn>0, 𝑑𝑛dn and 𝑒𝑛en with 𝑥𝑛 =𝑐𝑛/𝑑𝑛xn=cn/dn and 𝜀𝑛 =𝑒𝑛/𝑐𝑛εn=en/cn, satisfying

𝑎𝑛=𝑑𝑛−𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑛+1,𝑐𝑛+1=𝑐𝑛−𝑒𝑛,𝑑𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝑑𝑛,an=dn−encn+1,cn+1=cn−en,dn+1=andn,

and the proof of that lemma also gives 𝑐𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑛 −𝑑𝑛cn+1=ancn−dn. Under the dictionary (𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛,𝐸𝑛) =(𝑐𝑛,𝑑𝑛,𝑒𝑛)(Cn,Dn,En)=(cn,dn,en) these are exactly the objects of Section 4: the first relation is the centring map ctrctr rewritten as 𝑒𝑛 =𝑑𝑛 −(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝑐𝑛en=dn−(an−1)cn, the second is Proposition 4.1, the third is the denominator update, and the fourth is the tail update. The lower-case 𝑒𝑛en of Section 4 is −𝐸𝑛−En, so it is the negative of Koizumi’s 𝑒𝑛en at an index where the centred state is negative.

His Theorem 3  [12] shows that his Conjecture 1 , that for a positive rational 𝑟r whose gap sequence satisfies 𝜀𝑛 →0εn→0 one has 𝜀𝑛 =0εn=0 for all large 𝑛n, is equivalent to an affirmative answer to the question of Erdős and Graham recorded as his Question 1 , which is Problem 1.1 above. Two of the implications proved below have prior art in these canonical coordinates: his Lemma 3, that 𝜀𝑛 =0εn=0 forces 𝜀𝑛+1 =0εn+1=0, is the absorption of Theorem 5.8, and his Proposition 1(2), that 𝜀𝑛 ≥0εn≥0 for all large 𝑛n forces 𝜀𝑛 =0εn=0 for all large 𝑛n, is the descent of Theorem 8.1. These appear in canonical coordinates in [12]. Koizumi attributes Proposition 1(2) to Badea. Its contrapositive says that a counterexample must have negative errors infinitely often; it assumes the sign is eventually nonnegative, while Theorem 12.1 below assumes only that the negative part is eventually bounded, which admits sign changes of bounded depth at every scale.

The growth hypothesis in Problem 1.1 is calibrated by two facts about Sylvester’s sequence. It satisfies 𝑎𝑛 ≈𝑐2𝑛0an≈c02n with 𝑐0 =1.2640847…c0=1.2640847…, and shifting it further produces sequences with 𝑎𝑛 ≈𝐶2𝑛an≈C2n for arbitrarily large 𝐶C whose reciprocals still sum to a rational number [7]. The classical sufficient condition for irrationality, lim𝑛𝑎1/2𝑛𝑛 =∞limnan1/2n=∞, is therefore sharp. Kovač and Tao identify that condition as folklore  [7]; they attribute the sharpness observation to Erdős (1975). A sequence with 𝑎𝑛/𝑎2𝑛−1 →1an/an−12→1 has 𝑎1/2𝑛𝑛an1/2n convergent, so that criterion says nothing about the sequences of Problem 1.1, and rationality is genuinely possible there. Sylvester’s sequence is A000058 in the OEIS and its shifts A129871. For the recent literature on irrationality of Ahmes series we refer to Kovač and Tao [7], who resolve several problems of Erdős and Graham drawn from the same two sources cited above, and whose introduction gives a sample of the intermediate work, including Sándor (1984) and Badea (1987). They do not treat Problem #243; the rigidity conclusion asked for there is not among their results.

Crmarić and Kovač [18] address the neighbouring Problem #270, not Problem #243. Allowing integer 𝑓(𝑛) →∞f(n)→∞ in ∑𝑛(∏𝑓(𝑛)𝑗=1(𝑛 +𝑗))−1∑n(∏j=1f(n)(n+j))−1 gives every positive real value; imposing nondecreasing 𝑓f gives a measure-zero value set. The latter assertion does not rule out individual rational values. Their extension of Kakeya’s subsum argument explains why decay alone need not force irrationality when the summands remain freely selectable. The present exact denominator recurrence imposes additional compatibility, so neither direction is an implication between their theorem and ours.

The Formal Conjectures collection contains a mathematically equivalent unproved declaration, up to its zero-based indexing  . Its summand is ℚQ-valued, so Lean’s Summable hypothesis asserts the existence of a sum in ℚQ; the finite indexing shift changes that sum only by a rational prefix. The declaration therefore does encode the rationality premise, but its proof is sorry. Its role here is statement-level prior art; it supplies no proof authority, and the development in this note is independent of it. The checked results in this project include the state implications and the specified original-coordinate transfer theorems; they are not confined to the state system. Earlier formal work on the remainder method should also be distinguished from a solution of this problem: Koutsoukou-Argyraki and Li’s Archive of Formal Proofs entry [19] records an Isabelle/HOL formalisation of Erdős–Straus (1974), Theorem 2.1, Corollary 2.10 and Theorem 3.1. That is formal prior art for those classical criteria, not an existing formal proof of Erdős #243.

Results and proof status.

The cubic-rate theorem (Theorem 2.1) is an ordinary irrationality proof with formalised components. The bounded-negative theorem (Theorem 12.1) and the scalar finite-mass theorem (Theorem 13.1) have checked declarations. The checked canonical product- and LCM-defect theorems include their analytic transfer. The complete weighted-record statement has a proof source in the separate release; that source is not part of the main-repository build documented here. For the further record criteria, each evidence paragraph identifies the ordinary argument and the checked lemma it uses. In particular, Lemma 7.7 below proves the canonical odd-prime-power supply on the page; its new proof is not included in the inherited Lean receipt. The static-model conclusions in Section 14 are likewise ordinary results.

The additional bound or summability assumption is not supplied by the problem’s hypotheses. The record-excess equivalence therefore identifies an obligation; it does not discharge it. In the stable-gcd case the record-increment theorem gives a positive lower bound for the log-log coefficient, not necessarily an infinite coefficient. All nontermination conclusions retain the failure of eventual Sylvester behaviour as a hypothesis.

The proof of bounded-negative rigidity can be read independently of the cubic argument: exact tail updates, absorption, gcd stabilisation, persistent coprimality and a first crossing of a Chinese-remainder block. The finite-mass proof instead uses a bounded infinite product and descent of positive integers.

The remaining exclusions sharpen this boundary. By Theorem 5.8, a counterexample has 𝐸𝑛 ≠0En≠0 for every large 𝑛n. By Theorem 8.1 it cannot have 𝐸E eventually nonnegative. If its tail is all negative, Theorems 9.2 and 10.1 exclude, respectively, constant magnitude and periodic magnitude in the stated regime 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an with positive drift; they are not a classification of a mixed-sign tail. Under normalised vanishing, Theorems 12.1 and 13.1 show that the negative part is neither bounded nor of finite normalised mass. What survives is stated in Section 14.

Structure

There are three independent reading routes. For the cubic theorem, read Section 2, following the chain: integer tail, polynomial extraction, primitive cubic, transport square, scale classification, modulo-seven contradiction. For bounded-negative rigidity, read Sections 4, 5, 11 and 12; neither the cubic field nor the energy criterion is needed. For record criteria, read Sections 6 and 7, keeping LCM and primitive records distinct.

Section 13 is the short scalar product argument. Sections 9–10 retain earlier special cases and their formal sources. Section 14 separates necessary conditions on an actual reciprocal tail from statements about static avoidance models; it now answers the draft’s two auxiliary barrier questions under their stated hypotheses. Appendix A maps formal sources, and Appendix B explains the finite residue reduction. Pinned source links identify proof locations, not an assertion that every surrounding paragraph has been formalised.

The centred integer state

The three maps defined next carry out the two steps announced at the end of Section 1. The first two clear denominators along the sequence, so that a rational reciprocal sum leaves a sequence of integers; the third subtracts from that integer the value it takes on Sylvester’s sequence, leaving one number whose vanishing is the whole question. All three are maps between integer tuples and carry no hypothesis of any kind. The recurrences they encode are Koizumi’s [12]; the defect, scaling and two-step identities below are algebraic consequences of them in the conventions of the formal sources.

For 𝑎,𝐷,𝐶 ∈ℤa,D,C∈Z define

den⁡(𝑎,𝐷)=𝑎𝐷,tail⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)=𝑎𝐶−𝐷,ctr⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)=𝐷−(𝑎−1)𝐶,den⁡(a,D)=aD,tail⁡(a,D,C)=aC−D,ctr⁡(a,D,C)=D−(a−1)C,

the denominator update, the tail update, and the centred state. Given a sequence (𝑎𝑛)(an) of integers, whose terms we call the multipliers, we write 𝐷𝑛+1 =den⁡(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛)Dn+1=den⁡(an,Dn) for the denominator state, 𝐶𝑛+1 =tail⁡(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛)Cn+1=tail⁡(an,Dn,Cn) for the tail state, and 𝐸𝑛 =ctr⁡(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛)En=ctr⁡(an,Dn,Cn) for the centred state, also called the error. The word centred records what the third map does: it measures 𝐷𝑛Dn against (𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛(an−1)Cn, and 𝐷𝑛 =(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛Dn=(an−1)Cn holds at every index on Sylvester’s sequence (Example 4.2), so 𝐸E is a deviation from that sequence rather than a size. At an index where 𝐸𝑛 <0En<0 we write 𝑒𝑛 = −𝐸𝑛 >0en=−En>0 and call it the magnitude of the error there.

Proposition 4.1 (update law). tail⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶) =𝐶 −ctr⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)tail⁡(a,D,C)=C−ctr⁡(a,D,C); that is, 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝐶𝑛 −𝐸𝑛Cn+1=Cn−En.

Proof. 𝐶 −(𝐷 −(𝑎 −1)𝐶) =𝑎𝐶 −𝐷C−(D−(a−1)C)=aC−D. ◻

Formalised as the update law. The state therefore moves by exactly the error at each step, which is what makes the sign of 𝐸E decisive: where 𝐸E is positive the state falls, where 𝐸E is negative it rises, and where 𝐸E vanishes it is stationary.

Example 4.2 (the Sylvester orbit). Take 𝑎𝑛 =2,3,7,43,1807,…an=2,3,7,43,1807,… with 𝑎𝑛+1 =𝑎2𝑛 −𝑎𝑛 +1an+1=an2−an+1, and start the state at 𝐷0 =𝐶0 =1D0=C0=1. The two updates give

𝑛n 𝑎𝑛an 𝐷𝑛Dn 𝐶𝑛Cn 𝐸𝑛En
00 22 11 11 00
11 33 22 11 00
22 77 66 11 00
33 4343 4242 11 00
44 18071807 18061806 11 00

and 𝐷𝑛 =𝑎𝑛 −1Dn=an−1 with 𝐶𝑛 =1Cn=1 at every index: if 𝐷𝑛 =𝑎𝑛 −1Dn=an−1 and 𝐶𝑛 =1Cn=1 then 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛 −(𝑎𝑛 −1) =1Cn+1=an−(an−1)=1 and 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛(𝑎𝑛 −1) =𝑎𝑛+1 −1Dn+1=an(an−1)=an+1−1. Hence 𝐸𝑛 =𝐷𝑛 −(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛 =0En=Dn−(an−1)Cn=0 throughout and the tail state never moves, which is Proposition 4.1 in the stationary case.

The canonical reciprocal-tail interpretation.

Let 𝑇𝑛 =∑𝑘≥𝑛1/𝑎𝑘Tn=∑k≥n1/ak and suppose 𝑇0 ∈ℚT0∈Q. Put 𝐷0D0 equal to a common denominator and 𝐷𝑛 =𝐷0𝑎0⋯𝑎𝑛−1Dn=D0a0⋯an−1, and set 𝐶𝑛 =𝐷𝑛𝑇𝑛Cn=DnTn. Then 𝐶𝑛 ∈ℤCn∈Z for every 𝑛n, and from 𝑇𝑛 =1/𝑎𝑛 +𝑇𝑛+1Tn=1/an+Tn+1 one gets 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝐶𝑛 −𝐷𝑛Cn+1=anCn−Dn, which is the tail update. On Sylvester’s sequence 𝑇𝑛 =1/(𝑎𝑛 −1)Tn=1/(an−1) exactly, so 𝐷𝑛 =(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛Dn=(an−1)Cn and 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0: the centred state measures deviation from the Sylvester tail identity, and it vanishes identically on the Sylvester orbit.

The elementary identities in ReciprocalTailRigidity.lean are stated for an abstract integer system. Their canonical reciprocal-tail interpretation is supplied separately by the checked PaperCompleteR7 modules, including the product-defect transfer. The natural-state identities used in this passage include the tail realisation, the denominator realisation, and the signed update. Keeping these levels separate makes the hypotheses of each implication visible without suggesting that the analytic interpretation is absent.

The series itself is reached by three further declarations, which were absent from earlier revisions of this note. Write 𝐶𝑛/𝐷𝑛Cn/Dn for the real ratio carried by the natural state, the tail ratio. Given 𝑎𝑛 >0an>0, 𝐷𝑛 >0Dn>0, 𝐶𝑛+1 +𝐷𝑛 =𝑎𝑛𝐶𝑛Cn+1+Dn=anCn and 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛Dn+1=anDn, one exact step removes 1/𝑎𝑛1/an from that ratio one-step reciprocal identity, finite iteration telescopes to a partial sum plus the endpoint ratio finite telescoping, and convergence of the endpoint ratio to zero identifies the infinite sum the series realisation: ∑𝑛1/𝑎𝑛∑n1/an then has sum 𝐶0/𝐷0C0/D0. These three carry no growth hypothesis, no centring hypothesis and no rationality hypothesis, and they exclude nothing. They close the loop between the integer system and the series that motivates it. These three declarations concern state-to-series realisation. The opposite direction, construction from a rational reciprocal sum, is an ordinary calculation here and is also supplied by the separate canonical declarations in PaperCompleteR7. It must not be declared unchecked merely because it is absent from this abstract-state module.

Proposition 4.3 (scale equivariance). For every 𝑠,𝑎,𝐷,𝐶 ∈ℤs,a,D,C∈Z,

den⁡(𝑎,𝑠𝐷)=𝑠den⁡(𝑎,𝐷),tail⁡(𝑎,𝑠𝐷,𝑠𝐶)=𝑠tail⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶),den⁡(a,sD)=sden⁡(a,D),tail⁡(a,sD,sC)=stail⁡(a,D,C),
ctr⁡(𝑎,𝑠𝐷,𝑠𝐶)=𝑠ctr⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶).ctr⁡(a,sD,sC)=sctr⁡(a,D,C).

Formalised as the denominator equivariance, the tail equivariance, and the centred equivariance. The system depends only on the ray through (𝐷,𝐶)(D,C). This is used twice below: once to normalise the finite search of Appendix B, and once, in Theorem 10.1, as the induction step that removes common scale.

The defect identity and its two consequences

Section 4 connects the Sylvester recurrence to the error in one direction only: on Sylvester’s sequence the error vanishes. The converse is what the problem needs, and it comes from a single identity, which expresses the deviation of 𝑎𝑛+1an+1 from the Sylvester successor, multiplied by the tail state 𝐶𝑛+1Cn+1, as a combination of the errors at 𝑛n and at 𝑛 +1n+1, the first weighted by 𝑎2𝑛an2. Its two consequences are Theorem 5.7, in which an eventually vanishing error forces the recurrence provided the tail state is eventually nonzero, and Theorem 5.8, in which, under strict centring (the condition |𝐸𝑛| <𝐶𝑛|En|<Cn at every index), one vanishing error propagates to every later index.

Write def⁡(𝑎,𝑎′) =𝑎′ −syl⁡(𝑎)def⁡(a,a′)=a′−syl⁡(a) for the deviation of the next term from the Sylvester successor, the Sylvester defect.

Theorem 5.1 (defect identity). For all 𝑎,𝑎′,𝐷,𝐶 ∈ℤa,a′,D,C∈Z,

def⁡(𝑎,𝑎′)⋅tail⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)=𝑎2ctr⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)−ctr⁡(𝑎′,den⁡(𝑎,𝐷),tail⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)),def⁡(a,a′)⋅tail⁡(a,D,C)=a2ctr⁡(a,D,C)−ctr⁡(a′,den⁡(a,D),tail⁡(a,D,C)),

that is, Δ𝑛 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝑎2𝑛𝐸𝑛 −𝐸𝑛+1ΔnCn+1=an2En−En+1.

Proof. A direct expansion: both sides equal 𝑎′𝑎𝐶 −𝑎′𝐷 −𝑎3𝐶 +𝑎2𝐷 +𝑎2𝐶 −𝑎𝐷 −𝑎𝐶 +𝐷a′aC−a′D−a3C+a2D+a2C−aD−aC+D. ◻

Formalised as the defect identity. It is a polynomial identity in four indeterminates, with no hypothesis of any kind, and it carries the whole argument twice over: once for rigidity, and once for absorption.

Example 5.2 (one defect and the error it creates). Continue Example 4.2 but replace 𝑎3 =43a3=43 by 𝑎3 =44a3=44. The states 𝐷3 =42D3=42 and 𝐶3 =1C3=1 are unchanged, since they depend only on 𝑎0,𝑎1,𝑎2a0,a1,a2, and 𝐸2 =0E2=0 still. The defect is Δ2 =𝑎3 −syl⁡(𝑎2) =44 −43 =1Δ2=a3−syl⁡(a2)=44−43=1, and 𝐸3 =𝐷3 −(𝑎3 −1)𝐶3 =42 −43 = −1E3=D3−(a3−1)C3=42−43=−1, so the identity reads

Δ2𝐶3=1⋅1=1=49⋅0−(−1)=𝑎22𝐸2−𝐸3.Δ2C3=1⋅1=1=49⋅0−(−1)=a22E2−E3.

By Proposition 4.1 the tail state then rises, 𝐶4 =𝐶3 −𝐸3 =2C4=C3−E3=2. A single unit of defect at one index has produced a negative error of magnitude 11 at the next, and the state has started to climb.

Theorem 5.3 (two vanishing errors force the step). Let 𝑎,𝑎′,𝐷,𝐶 ∈ℤa,a′,D,C∈Z with tail⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶) ≠0tail⁡(a,D,C)≠0. If ctr⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶) =0ctr⁡(a,D,C)=0 and ctr⁡(𝑎′,den⁡(𝑎,𝐷),tail⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)) =0ctr⁡(a′,den⁡(a,D),tail⁡(a,D,C))=0, then 𝑎′ =syl⁡(𝑎)a′=syl⁡(a).

Proof. By Theorem 5.1 the product def⁡(𝑎,𝑎′) ⋅tail⁡(𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)def⁡(a,a′)⋅tail⁡(a,D,C) is zero, and the second factor is nonzero by hypothesis. ◻

Formalised as the local rigidity step. The hypothesis 𝐶𝑛+1 ≠0Cn+1≠0 is not removable: at 𝐶𝑛+1 =0Cn+1=0 the identity gives no information about 𝑎′a′.

Two-step cancellation and feedback

The one-step state equations hide a second-order constraint once the raw numerator is reduced at two consecutive stages. Write 𝑢,𝑢1,𝑢2u,u1,u2 for the primitive numerator coordinates, 𝑣,𝑣1v,v1 for the corresponding denominator coordinates, and ℎ,ℎ1h,h1 for the two common factors removed in reduction. If the two steps have multipliers 𝑎,𝑎1a,a1, then the exact hypotheses are

ℎ𝑢1+𝑣=𝑎𝑢,ℎ𝑣1=𝑎𝑣,ℎ1𝑢2+𝑣1=𝑎1𝑢1.hu1+v=au,hv1=av,h1u2+v1=a1u1.

Theorem 5.4 (two-step primitive recurrence). Let 𝑎,𝑎1,𝑢,𝑢1,𝑢2,𝑣,𝑣1,ℎ,ℎ1a,a1,u,u1,u2,v,v1,h,h1 be integers satisfying

ℎ𝑢1+𝑣=𝑎𝑢,ℎ𝑣1=𝑎𝑣,ℎ1𝑢2+𝑣1=𝑎1𝑢1.hu1+v=au,hv1=av,h1u2+v1=a1u1.

Then 𝑎2𝑢 +ℎℎ1𝑢2 =ℎ(𝑎 +𝑎1)𝑢1a2u+hh1u2=h(a+a1)u1.

Proof. Multiply the first equation by 𝑎a, replace 𝑎𝑣av using the second equation, and then replace ℎ1𝑢2 +𝑣1h1u2+v1 using the third. The remaining terms factor as the displayed right-hand side. ◻

This is the two-step primitive recurrence. The hard point is keeping both changing cancellation factors visible. It is an elimination identity for two exact steps, not a new assumption. It remains non-autonomous and cannot by itself force 𝑎1 =𝑎2 −𝑎 +1a1=a2−a+1; Lemma 5.6 specifies what it forgets modulo a fixed old denominator.

There is a complementary integer identity when the relevant step is cancellation-free. Put 𝑞 =𝑎𝑝 −𝑝1q=ap−p1, and suppose the next primitive coordinate satisfies

𝑝2+𝑎2𝑝=(𝑎+𝑎1)𝑝1.p2+a2p=(a+a1)p1.

Then

Theorem 5.5 (cancellation-free curvature identity). Let 𝑎,𝑎1,𝑝,𝑝1,𝑝2,𝑞a,a1,p,p1,p2,q be integers with 𝑞 =𝑎𝑝 −𝑝1q=ap−p1 and 𝑝2 +𝑎2𝑝 =(𝑎 +𝑎1)𝑝1p2+a2p=(a+a1)p1. Then

𝑞2+(𝑝𝑝2−𝑝21)=(𝑎1−𝑎)𝑝𝑝1.q2+(pp2−p12)=(a1−a)pp1.

The square 𝑞2q2 is the local remainder, while 𝑝𝑝2 −𝑝21pp2−p12 is a discrete curvature term. The right side records the change in multiplier, so the identity supplies a diagnostic for an anti-shadowing argument without asserting a sign or a global monotonicity. It is checked as the cancellation-free curvature square; no global anti-shadowing conclusion is claimed.

Finally, the reduced denominator transport has a precise realisability condition. Let 𝑒,𝑒1e,e1 be centred errors and let ΔΔ be the Sylvester defect. If

ℎ𝑢1=𝑢−𝑒,ℎ𝑒1=𝑎2𝑒−Δ(𝑢−𝑒),hu1=u−e,he1=a2e−Δ(u−e),

then the transport equality

ℎ((𝑎1−1)𝑢1+𝑒1)=𝑎((𝑎−1)𝑢+𝑒)h((a1−1)u1+e1)=a((a−1)u+e)

has mismatch which factors through 𝑢 −𝑒u−e. Consequently, when 𝑢 −𝑒 ≠0u−e≠0,

ℎ((𝑎1−1)𝑢1+𝑒1)=𝑎((𝑎−1)𝑢+𝑒)⟺𝑎1=𝑎2−𝑎+1+Δ.h((a1−1)u1+e1)=a((a−1)u+e)⟺a1=a2−a+1+Δ.

This is the exact feedback transport equivalence, obtained from the factored defect at feedback transport defect. The nonzero-raw-numerator hypothesis is essential: if 𝑢 −𝑒 =0u−e=0, the factorised mismatch cannot identify 𝑎1a1.

The identities hold under the local hypotheses displayed in their statements. It is their proposed global applications, not the identities, that would need additional information, such as control of cancellation or a sign estimate for the curvature. No such information is deduced here for an arbitrary rational near-quadratic tail.

Lemma 5.6 (saturation modulo an old denominator). Let 𝑀 ≥2M≥2. Any finite word 𝑟0,…,𝑟𝑘r0,…,rk of units modulo 𝑀M is compatible with the cancellation-free recurrences modulo 𝑀M, with all reduced denominator residues equal to zero. Consequently the eliminated two-step identity alone imposes no further restriction on such unit words when the multiplier residues are free.

Proof. Set 𝑣𝑖 ≡0(mod𝑀)vi≡0(modM) and choose 𝑎𝑖 ≡𝑟𝑖+1𝑟−1𝑖(mod𝑀)ai≡ri+1ri−1(modM). Then 𝑟𝑖+1 +𝑣𝑖 ≡𝑎𝑖𝑟𝑖ri+1+vi≡airi and 𝑣𝑖+1 ≡𝑎𝑖𝑣𝑖vi+1≡aivi. Eliminating 𝑣𝑖vi gives the two-step identity automatically. ◻

This is finite residue compatibility, not existence of a positive integer orbit, much less a canonical rational tail with near-quadratic growth. For 𝑀 ∣𝑣𝑇M∣vT on a clean tail, the actual 𝑢𝑛un are indeed units modulo 𝑀M. Useful further restrictions must therefore retain information discarded here: for example multiplier size, changing moduli, or primes outside the old denominator. The square restriction used in the cubic proof concerns precisely a prime at which a middle numerator vanishes.

Theorem 5.7 (sequence form). Let 𝑎,𝐷,𝐶 :ℕ →ℤa,D,C:N→Z satisfy 𝐷𝑛+1 =den⁡(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛)Dn+1=den⁡(an,Dn) and 𝐶𝑛+1 =tail⁡(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛)Cn+1=tail⁡(an,Dn,Cn). If 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n and 𝐶𝑛+1 ≠0Cn+1≠0 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n, then 𝑎𝑛+1 =𝑎2𝑛 −𝑎𝑛 +1an+1=an2−an+1 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n.

Formalised as the eventual Sylvester recurrence. The proof is routine: take the larger of the two thresholds and apply Theorem 5.3 at each later index. Every later section is directed at the hypothesis of this theorem, that is, at forcing 𝐸E to vanish eventually.

The defect identity has a second consequence, which is what makes a single vanishing error worth having.

Theorem 5.8 (zero is absorbing). Let 𝑎,𝐶,𝐷 :ℕ →ℕa,C,D:N→N be an exact natural orbit, so 𝐶𝑛+1 +𝐷𝑛 =𝑎𝑛𝐶𝑛Cn+1+Dn=anCn and 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛Dn+1=anDn, and let 𝐸𝑛 =ctr⁡(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛)En=ctr⁡(an,Dn,Cn). Suppose the centring is strict, |𝐸𝑛| <𝐶𝑛|En|<Cn for every 𝑛n. If 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 then 𝐸𝑛+1 =0En+1=0.

Proof. Putting 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 in Theorem 5.1 gives Δ𝑛𝐶𝑛+1 = −𝐸𝑛+1ΔnCn+1=−En+1, so 𝐶𝑛+1Cn+1 divides 𝐸𝑛+1En+1. A multiple of 𝐶𝑛+1Cn+1 of absolute value smaller than 𝐶𝑛+1Cn+1 is zero, and |𝐸𝑛+1| <𝐶𝑛+1|En+1|<Cn+1 by hypothesis. ◻

Formalised as the absorption of a vanishing centred state, with the companion contrapositive along a tail: if zero is absorbing beyond some index and 𝐸E does not vanish eventually, then 𝐸E is nowhere zero beyond that index.

Absorption changes the shape of the problem. Either 𝐸E hits zero once and stays there, or it is never zero. Sections 9 and 10 address the special all-negative case only. The mixed-sign analysis in Sections 12 and 13 instead separates cofinally negative errors from an eventually positive tail.

Weighted first crossings of LCM records

This section recovers the weighted record criterion used by the short note. It is an exact criterion for Problem 1.1, stated under the hypotheses of that problem and no others, and it is reached by a first-crossing argument rather than by a hypothesis on the negative part. Only steps setting a new LCM numerator record contribute, a fixed LCM-scale baseline may be subtracted, and the remaining mass may be logarithmically discounted.

Evidence.

The proof below is ordinary mathematics. The first-crossing arithmetic has formalised components in LcmRecordExcess.lean. In addition, the separate release contains the full real-weight canonical criterion and its natural-weight version. These release sources contain proof bodies, but they are outside the supplied successful main-repository build; a Comparator configuration alone is not a replay receipt. The finite-orbit data retained with the source are diagnostic examples, not a proof of termination for all rational seeds.

The criterion moves the finiteness obligation from every step to record steps, with a fixed baseline subtracted. The inherited eventual-nonnegative case is Koizumi’s Proposition 1(2); the first-crossing proof also treats mixed signs. Proposition 7.15 concerns a deliberately weaker avoidance model. Its walks do not preserve all the prime-by-prime coprimality and exact denominator feedback of a canonical orbit. Consequently it is not an impossibility theorem for every coprimality-based approach. What remains is to derive a record budget from the exact recurrence, or find another contradiction on a nonterminal orbit.

Remaining obligation.

Derive finiteness of the displayed sum for one admissible weight and one fixed 𝐵B from rational denominator feedback, or contradict a nonterminal orbit by another route. The logarithmic discount weakens what suffices; it does not establish it.

Criteria in the record coordinates

The criterion of Section 6 lives in the LCM coordinates 𝑈𝑛 =𝐶𝑛/𝑀𝑛Un=Cn/Mn, where old divisors persist. The statements of this section live in the primitive coordinates, where old divisors can be deleted. They are collected here because each is an equivalence, a dichotomy, or an unconditional exclusion, and because each sharpens the profile of a counterexample in a direction the earlier sections do not reach. The underlying tools are the Chinese remainder theorem, persistence of prime-power divisors and weighted first-crossing counting; the LCM compression and the reuse comparison are attributed in Section 6.

Primitive coordinates.

This theorem is incomparable with the two-unit record theorem: a record-setting jump of size at most two bounds 𝑠𝑛 ≤2sn≤2 rather than 𝑠𝑛 ≤1sn≤1, and 𝑠𝑛 ≤1sn≤1 allows arbitrarily large record-setting jumps after a drawdown. 8𝑝𝐿=16𝑄≤1,8𝑝+8√𝐿≤8√2(1+1/𝑝)<16.8pL=16Q≤1,8p+8L≤82(1+1/p)<16.

Evidence.

The separate release contains the integer protected-epoch inequality and its counting lemmas. This revision imported that module into the public ErdosProblems root; AxiomAudit prints protected_epoch_energy_integer against the standard axioms. The canonical supply, real-valued bound and assembled energy equivalence above remain ordinary paper arguments; the Lean inequality is the checked integer form, not a checked transcription of the whole assembled theorem. The checked main-repository declaration the two-unit record-rise implication retains a supply premise: arbitrarily late 𝑠s admit an odd 𝑝𝑘 ∣𝑣𝑠pk∣vs with 3𝑅𝑠 <𝑝𝑘3Rs<pk. Lemma 7.7 supplies this premise in ordinary mathematics. The declaration itself has not thereby become an end-to-end checked canonical theorem. This distinction is about formal coverage, not an unfilled mathematical supply argument in the text.

A slow negative part, and the original coordinates

Theorem 7.11 (slow negative part). Let (𝑎,𝐶,𝐷)(a,C,D) be an exact natural orbit with 𝑎𝑛 >1an>1, 𝐶𝑛 >0Cn>0, 𝐷0 ≥1D0≥1, under normalised vanishing. Suppose that for some 𝛿 ∈(0,1)δ∈(0,1) and all large 𝑛n with 𝐸𝑛 <0En<0 one has −𝐸𝑛 ≤(1 −𝛿)ℓ(𝐶𝑛)−En≤(1−δ)ℓ(Cn). Then 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 for all large 𝑛n, and 𝑎𝑛+1 =𝑎2𝑛 −𝑎𝑛 +1an+1=an2−an+1 for all large 𝑛n.

Theorem 12.1 is the case of a constant bound, since a constant is eventually below (1 −𝛿)ℓ(𝐶𝑛)(1−δ)ℓ(Cn).

Mechanism.

Normalised vanishing gives 𝐶𝑛+1 <32𝐶𝑛Cn+1<32Cn, hence ℓ(𝐶𝑛) ≤log2⁡𝑛 +𝑂(1)ℓ(Cn)≤log2⁡n+O(1), and 𝑎𝑛an grows at least geometrically. The multiplier overlap gcd(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛)gcd(an,Dn) is bounded by the next negative magnitude and therefore by ℓ(𝐶𝑛) +1ℓ(Cn)+1. Splitting 𝑎𝑛an into the part coprime to 𝐷𝑛Dn and the burnt part, a poor index supplies a burn prime with valuation above √𝑛n, and such primes are injective across a window, so a window [𝑇,2𝑇][T,2T] has at most 𝑇 +𝑂(1)T+O(1) poor indices. The first 𝐵B rich indices give 𝐵B pairwise-coprime moduli above any prescribed size, and the block form of the landing lemma applies.

Evidence.

Ordinary proof over the Lean core. The kernel-checked ingredients are the persistence of a common divisor, the overlap transport, the landing lemma and the coprime-block exclusion. The burn count and the choice of constants are ordinary mathematics. Corollary 7.4 supersedes this theorem on two axes, the drawdown-corrected observable and the inclusive constant, and this theorem is retained because its hypothesis is stated directly on 𝐸𝑛En.

Erdős and Straus require lim sup ≤0lim sup≤0 in the corresponding criterion, with the least common multiple in place of the product and the growth factor one index later, so their quantity is [𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛]𝑎−1𝑛+1(𝑎2𝑛+1/𝑎𝑛+2 −1)[a1,…,an]an+1−1(an+12/an+2−1) ; Koizumi’s Corollary 4(1) uses the product form [12]. It is the only place in this note where the machine-checked theorem is written in the vocabulary of the 1964 paper.

Reading.

Proposition 7.15 concerns avoidance of whole multiples, not coprimality to a composite modulus. The distinction matters: no integer in [2,5)[2,5) is coprime to 3030, although none is divisible by 3030. Thus this proposition alone does not disprove a coprime-walk extension of Theorem 11.3. Proposition 14.6 below gives a separate counterexample using sparse prime moduli. Under the additional scale ℓ(𝑚𝑗) =𝑗 +𝑂(1)ℓ(mj)=j+O(1), Theorem 14.7 determines the exact maximal-gap coefficient for whole-modulus avoidance. Its proof replaces the former numerical conjecture; the previously recorded finite value 1.81161.8116 for the Fermat family is not used. Neither static construction supplies an exact reciprocal-tail orbit.

The exact remaining obstacle.

Every criterion of this section leaves the same regime, which is

(1−𝛿)ℓ(𝐶𝑛) ≤ −𝐸𝑛 = 𝑜(𝐶𝑛)at infinitely many 𝑛,(1−δ)ℓ(Cn) ≤ −En = o(Cn)at infinitely many n,

with divergent normalised negative mass, unbounded record-amplified error, and infinitely many clean primitive record jumps of size at least three. These criteria do not exclude that regime. The residue-saturation lemma shows precisely one limitation of the fixed-old-modulus method; it is not an impossibility theorem about every future approach. A useful next target is interaction between new prime support, three consecutive numerators and the global height budget.

Descent when the error is nonnegative

The hypothesis of the theorem below is the update law of Proposition 4.1 read inside ℕN: the error is nonnegative at every index, so the tail state never rises. This is the easy case, and it is settled in three lines.

Theorem 8.1 (descent). Let 𝐶,𝐸 :ℕ →ℕC,E:N→N satisfy 𝐶𝑛+1 +𝐸𝑛 =𝐶𝑛Cn+1+En=Cn for every 𝑛n. Then 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n.

Proof. A one-line descent. The relation forces 𝐶𝑛+1 ≤𝐶𝑛Cn+1≤Cn, so 𝐶C is a nonincreasing sequence of natural numbers and is eventually equal to its minimum; beyond that index 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝐶𝑛Cn+1=Cn, and the relation gives 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0. ◻

Formalised as the stabilisation of the nonnegative error, on the eventual constancy of a nonincreasing sequence.

The hypothesis is exactly one-sidedness: 𝐶C and 𝐸E take values in ℕN. If 𝐸𝑛 <0En<0 at infinitely many indices then 𝐶C rises there, nothing descends, and the argument is unavailable. That is the whole difficulty, and the rest of this note is directed at it.

Excluding a constant negative magnitude

The exclusions in this section and the next concern infinite constant or periodic negative magnitudes, and they do not bound the length of a finite transient. Arbitrarily long constant transients occur on genuine rational orbits, by the flat-transient theorem of the working report on Problem #243 [9].

Suppose the error is negative with a constant magnitude, 𝐸𝑛 = −𝑚En=−m for a fixed 𝑚 >0m>0 and every 𝑛n. By Proposition 4.1 the state then climbs by exactly 𝑚m each step, so 𝐶𝑛 =𝑐 +𝑛𝑚Cn=c+nm with 𝑐 =𝐶0c=C0, and the definition of the centred state becomes a shape equation

𝐷𝑛+𝑚=(𝑎𝑛−1)(𝑐+𝑛𝑚).(5.1)(5.1)Dn+m=(an−1)(c+nm).

Together with 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛Dn+1=anDn this is a closed system in (𝑎,𝐷)(a,D), and it has no solutions. The following instance shows how the failure happens; the theorem then shows that it cannot be avoided.

Example 9.1 (the shape equation running until it fails). Take 𝑚 =𝑐 =1m=c=1, so that 𝐶𝑛 =1 +𝑛Cn=1+n and the shape equation (5.1) reads 𝐷𝑛 +1 =(𝑎𝑛 −1)(1 +𝑛)Dn+1=(an−1)(1+n), and take 𝐷0 =1D0=1. Each step is now determined: at 𝑛 =0n=0 the equation reads 2 =(𝑎0 −1) ⋅12=(a0−1)⋅1, so 𝑎0 =3a0=3, and 𝐷1 =𝑎0𝐷0 =3D1=a0D0=3; at 𝑛 =1n=1 it reads 4 =(𝑎1 −1) ⋅24=(a1−1)⋅2, so 𝑎1 =3a1=3, and 𝐷2 =𝑎1𝐷1 =9D2=a1D1=9; at 𝑛 =2n=2 it reads 10 =(𝑎2 −1) ⋅310=(a2−1)⋅3, which has no integer solution, and the orbit stops. Longer prefixes occur for other starting values: the finite search recorded in Appendix B found none longer than 1717 among the initial states below 50005000.

Theorem 9.2 (no constant negative magnitude). There is no pair of sequences 𝑎,𝐷 :ℕ →ℕa,D:N→N with 𝑎𝑛 ≥2an≥2 for all 𝑛n satisfying 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛Dn+1=anDn and (5.1), for any 𝑚 >0m>0 and any 𝑐c. The same holds if the shape only begins at some index.

Proof when 𝑐c and 𝑚m are coprime. Assume first gcd(𝑐,𝑚) =1gcd(c,m)=1. Two facts about the multipliers do all the work, and the difficulty lies in the fact that they concern the same finite set of primes from opposite directions: the first makes every multiplier meet that set, the second lets each prime of the set meet at most one multiplier.

Every 𝑎𝑗aj shares a prime with 𝑚m. Suppose gcd(𝑎𝑗,𝑚) =1gcd(aj,m)=1. Then 𝑚m is invertible modulo 𝑎𝑗aj, so some 𝑛n has 𝑐 +𝑛𝑚 ≡0c+nm≡0, that is 𝑎𝑗 ∣𝐶𝑛aj∣Cn; and 𝑎𝑗 ∣𝐷𝑛aj∣Dn for every 𝑛 >𝑗n>j, since 𝐷D is multiplicative with 𝑎𝑗aj among its factors. Choosing such an 𝑛n beyond 𝑗j and reading (5.1) modulo 𝑎𝑗aj gives 𝑎𝑗 ∣𝑚aj∣m, contradicting gcd(𝑎𝑗,𝑚) =1gcd(aj,m)=1 and 𝑎𝑗 ≥2aj≥2.

A prime divisor of 𝑚m occurs in at most one 𝑎𝑗aj. Suppose 𝑝 ∣𝑚p∣m and 𝑝 ∣𝑎𝑗p∣aj. For 𝑛 >𝑗n>j we have 𝑝 ∣𝐷𝑛p∣Dn, so (5.1) gives (𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛 ≡0(mod𝑝)(an−1)Cn≡0(modp). Now 𝐶𝑛 =𝑐 +𝑛𝑚 ≡𝑐Cn=c+nm≡c, and 𝑝 ∤𝑐p∤c because 𝑝 ∣𝑚p∣m and gcd(𝑐,𝑚) =1gcd(c,m)=1; hence 𝑝 ∣𝑎𝑛 −1p∣an−1, so 𝑝 ∤𝑎𝑛p∤an. Thus 𝑝p cannot divide any later multiplier.

The two facts are incompatible. Each of the infinitely many multipliers needs a prime divisor of 𝑚m, and each prime divisor of 𝑚m serves at most one multiplier, while 𝑚m has only finitely many prime divisors. ◻

The case gcd(𝑐,𝑚) =1gcd(c,m)=1 is the scale-primitive exclusion. The special case 𝑚 =𝑐 =1m=c=1, worked through in Example 9.1, where 𝑚m has no prime divisors at all and the first fact is immediately contradictory, is recorded separately as the normalised exclusion.

Removing the scale. For general 𝑐c, put 𝑔 =gcd(𝑐,𝑚)g=gcd(c,m). Equation (5.1) shows 𝑔 ∣𝐷𝑛g∣Dn for every 𝑛n, so dividing 𝐷D, 𝑐c and 𝑚m by 𝑔g leaves a system of the same shape with coprime data, which the previous case excludes. ◻

Formalised as the exclusion at every scale, and the eventual form, obtained by shifting the orbit to the first constant index, as the eventual exclusion.

Theorem 9.2 excludes a centred state that is eventually constant and negative, at every magnitude and every scale. It says nothing about a negative state whose magnitude changes, and the argument genuinely uses constancy: the finiteness of the set of prime divisors of 𝑚m is what the pigeonhole uses, and a varying magnitude presents a fresh set at each index.

Excluding a periodic negative magnitude

The next case allows the magnitude to vary, provided it repeats. Write 𝑒𝑛 = −𝐸𝑛 >0en=−En>0 for the magnitude, as in Section 4, so that 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝐶𝑛 +𝑒𝑛Cn+1=Cn+en; suppose 𝑒e has period ℎh, meaning 𝑒𝑛+ℎ =𝑒𝑛en+h=en for every 𝑛n, and that the state gains a fixed drift 𝑀 >0M>0 over one period, meaning 𝐶𝑛+ℎ =𝐶𝑛 +𝑀Cn+h=Cn+M for every 𝑛n.

At ℎ =1h=1 this says that the magnitude is constant and that 𝑀M is its value, which is the situation of Section 9; Theorem 9.2 already excludes it, and does so without the extra hypothesis 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an imposed below. The new content is ℎ ≥2h≥2.

Section 9 could run its pigeonhole on the prime divisors of the single number 𝑚m. Here the magnitude changes inside a period, and the number available to run it on is the drift 𝑀M. Three lemmas replace the two facts of Section 9. The first is that multipliers persist: every 𝑎𝑗aj divides every strictly later denominator state, the persistence of a multiplier. The second is a lock: a prime already dividing 𝐷D and also dividing the current multiplier is forced into the next tail state, the one-step lock, and once present in both 𝐷D and 𝐶C it stays in every later 𝐷D, 𝐶C and magnitude, the persistence of a lock. The third transports a lock backwards through the period: if a divisor of the drift 𝑀M occurs in two multipliers, it is a common divisor of 𝐶0C0 and of every magnitude, the repeated-divisor transport, using that both the period relation and the drift iterate over any number of periods, the iterated period and the iterated drift.

Theorem 10.1 (no periodic negative magnitude). Let 𝑎,𝐷,𝐶,𝑒 :ℕ →ℕa,D,C,e:N→N with 𝑎𝑛 ≥2an≥2, 𝑒𝑛 >0en>0 and 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an for every 𝑛n, satisfying

𝐷𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛+1=𝐶𝑛+𝑒𝑛,𝐷𝑛+𝑒𝑛=(𝑎𝑛−1)𝐶𝑛,Dn+1=anDn,Cn+1=Cn+en,Dn+en=(an−1)Cn,

and suppose 𝑒𝑛+ℎ =𝑒𝑛en+h=en and 𝐶𝑛+ℎ =𝐶𝑛 +𝑀Cn+h=Cn+M for some ℎ >0h>0 and 𝑀 >0M>0. This is impossible.

Proof. Strong induction on the drift 𝑀M. The difficulty lies in the fact that a repeated prime divisor of 𝑀M need not contradict anything directly. It instead forces a common scale on the whole orbit, which can be divided out, and the induction runs on the drift that the division reduces.

Suppose first that no prime divisor of 𝑀M is a common divisor of 𝐶0C0 and of every magnitude. Repeated-divisor transport then applies in the contrapositive: a prime divisor of 𝑀M occurring in two of the multipliers would be exactly such a common divisor, so each prime divisor of 𝑀M occurs in at most one multiplier. Against this, the argument of Section 9 run phase by phase (along a fixed residue class modulo ℎh the magnitude is constant and 𝐶C advances by 𝑀M at each period, so the multipliers of that phase meet an arithmetic progression exactly as in Section 9) makes every multiplier share a prime with 𝑀M. Since 𝑀M has only finitely many prime divisors and there are infinitely many multipliers, pigeonhole gives a contradiction.

Otherwise some prime 𝑝p divides 𝑀M, divides 𝐶0C0, and divides every magnitude. Then 𝑝 ∣𝐶𝑛p∣Cn for every 𝑛n, since 𝐶𝑛+1 =𝐶𝑛 +𝑒𝑛Cn+1=Cn+en and both summands on the right are divisible by 𝑝p, and the shape equation 𝐷𝑛 +𝑒𝑛 =(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛Dn+en=(an−1)Cn then gives 𝑝 ∣𝐷𝑛p∣Dn for every 𝑛n. Divide 𝐷D, 𝐶C and 𝑒e by 𝑝p. The multipliers are untouched, so 𝑎𝑛 ≥2an≥2 and 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an persist and the magnitudes stay positive; the three recurrences are homogeneous in (𝐷,𝐶,𝑒)(D,C,e) and so survive; the period is still ℎh; and the drift becomes 𝑀/𝑝 <𝑀M/p<M. The inductive hypothesis applies. ◻

The first of the two cases above is the phase-primitive exclusion, the induction is the exclusion at every scale, and the eventual form is the eventual exclusion.

The bound 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an is a genuine restriction and not a normalisation. It is the range in which a multiplier cannot divide its own phase magnitude, which is what the lock argument needs. It holds in the intended reading, where 𝑒𝑛en is a centred representative and 𝑎𝑛an grows quadratically, but it is assumed here and not derived. The drift hypothesis 𝑀 >0M>0 is also used: a periodic magnitude with zero drift would be identically zero, which is the case already settled by Section 8.

Remark. On the canonical orbit of , read through the dictionary of Section 3, the bound 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an holds eventually. Lemma 4(2) there gives the centring range −𝐶𝑛/2 ≤𝐸𝑛 <𝐶𝑛/2−Cn/2≤En<Cn/2, so 𝑒𝑛 =|𝐸𝑛| ≤𝐶𝑛/2en=|En|≤Cn/2 at a negative index, and the proof of Lemma 4(3) gives 𝐶𝑛+1 ≤32𝐶𝑛Cn+1≤32Cn  , hence the uniform bound 𝐶𝑛 ≤𝐶0(3/2)𝑛Cn≤C0(3/2)n. Against this, summability of ∑1/𝑎𝑛∑1/an forces 𝑎𝑛 →∞an→∞, and the growth hypothesis 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 →1an2/an+1→1 gives 𝑎𝑛+1 ≥𝑎2𝑛/2an+1≥an2/2 for all large 𝑛n, hence 𝑎𝑛+1 ≥2𝑎𝑛an+1≥2an once 𝑎𝑛 ≥4an≥4; so the multipliers grow at least geometrically with ratio 22 and outgrow the bound on 𝐶𝑛Cn, making 𝑒𝑛/𝑎𝑛en/an eventually small. Two caveats. Summability is used for this step, so the estimate is not available from the state recurrence alone; and the conclusion is eventual and not universal, whereas Theorem 10.1 imposes 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an at every index, so it is the eventual form of the exclusion cited above that applies. Under the periodicity hypothesis of Theorem 10.1 the estimate is in any case unnecessary, since a periodic magnitude is bounded while the multipliers tend to infinity.

Bounded rise cannot remain coprime to fresh moduli

Periodicity is still a strong assumption. Removing it needs a different kind of obstruction, and the one used here is a counting argument about where an integer sequence with bounded upward steps must land.

Lemma 11.1 (shifted blocks of consecutive multiples). Let 𝑚0,…,𝑚𝐵−1m0,…,mB−1 be pairwise coprime and at least 22. For every bound there is a 𝑡t beyond it with 𝑚𝑖 ∣𝑡 +𝑖mi∣t+i for each 𝑖 <𝐵i<B.

Proof. Standard Chinese remaindering: solve 𝑡 ≡ −𝑖(mod𝑚𝑖)t≡−i(modmi) simultaneously, then add multiples of ∏𝑖𝑚𝑖∏imi to pass the bound. ◻

Formalised as the shifted consecutive multiples.

Lemma 11.1 matches each modulus 𝑚𝑖mi to its own multiple 𝑡 +𝑖t+i inside a window of 𝐵B consecutive integers. Matchings of a set of integers to distinct multiples in an interval are the subject of Erdős Problem #650, solved by van Doorn, Li and Tang: for every set 𝑆S of 𝑘k positive integers, every open interval of length 2max𝑆2maxS contains distinct multiples of at least min(𝑘,⌈2√𝑘 ⌉)min(k,⌈2k⌉) elements of 𝑆S, and this count is optimal . Their extremal construction uses the same Chinese remaindering for moduli that need not be pairwise coprime, with their Claim 3.2 supplying the divisibility of residue differences by greatest common divisors that the generalised theorem requires [11]. The first-crossing argument below needs only the pairwise coprime case.

Example 11.2 (a block of three consecutive multiples). Take 𝐵 =3B=3 and (𝑚0,𝑚1,𝑚2) =(3,4,5)(m0,m1,m2)=(3,4,5). The congruences 𝑡 ≡0(mod3)t≡0(mod3), 𝑡 ≡3(mod4)t≡3(mod4) and 𝑡 ≡3(mod5)t≡3(mod5) hold exactly when 𝑡 ≡3(mod60)t≡3(mod60). At 𝑡 =3t=3 the block is 3,4,53,4,5 with 3 ∣33∣3, 4 ∣44∣4 and 5 ∣55∣5; at 𝑡 =63t=63 it is 63,64,6563,64,65 with 3 ∣633∣63, 4 ∣644∣64 and 5 ∣655∣65. A sequence of natural numbers that starts at 00, tends to infinity and rises by at most 33 at each step cannot step over the block {3,4,5}{3,4,5}: it has a first value at least 33, that value is at most 55, and every member of {3,4,5}{3,4,5} is divisible by one of the three moduli.

Theorem 11.3 (bounded rise cannot remain coprime to fresh moduli). Let 𝑢 :ℕ →ℕu:N→N tend to infinity with 𝑢𝑛+1 ≤𝑢𝑛 +𝐵un+1≤un+B for a fixed integer 𝐵 ≥1B≥1. Then 𝑢u cannot remain coprime to infinitely many fresh pairwise coprime moduli: there is no family of pairwise coprime 𝑚𝑖 ≥2mi≥2, one for each index, such that gcd(𝑚𝑖,𝑢𝑡) =1gcd(mi,ut)=1 whenever 𝑖 <𝑡i<t.

The time threshold in the proof is essential. The rise bound restricts upward jumps but permits arbitrary falls: for example, if 𝑀 ≥1M≥1, then 𝑢0 =𝑀u0=M, 𝑢1 =0u1=0, and 𝑢𝑛 =𝑛 −1un=n−1 for 𝑛 ≥1n≥1 satisfies the bound with 𝐵 =1B=1 and tends to infinity, although the large height 𝑀M is already attained at time 00.

Proof. Choose 𝑚0,…,𝑚𝐵−1m0,…,mB−1 and use Lemma 11.1 to find 𝑡 >max(𝑢0,…,𝑢𝐵)t>max(u0,…,uB) with 𝑚𝑖 ∣𝑡 +𝑖mi∣t+i for 0 ≤𝑖 <𝐵0≤i<B. Since 𝑢𝑛 →∞un→∞, there is a first 𝑛 >𝐵n>B with 𝑢𝑛 ≥𝑡un≥t. Minimality and the rise bound give

𝑡≤𝑢𝑛≤𝑢𝑛−1+𝐵<𝑡+𝐵.t≤un≤un−1+B<t+B.

Hence 𝑢𝑛 =𝑡 +𝑖un=t+i for some 0 ≤𝑖 <𝐵 <𝑛0≤i<B<n, so 𝑚𝑖 ∣𝑢𝑛mi∣un. The inequality 𝑖 <𝑛i<n now permits the avoidance hypothesis, which says gcd(𝑚𝑖,𝑢𝑛) =1gcd(mi,un)=1; this contradicts 𝑚𝑖 ≥2mi≥2. The argument uses the first crossing of the CRT block, not monotonicity of 𝑢u. ◻

Formalised as the bounded-rise barrier. The key point is that the two hypotheses pull against each other exactly: divergence forces 𝑢u to travel arbitrarily far, and bounded rise forbids it from stepping over a window of width 𝐵B. Uniformity of the bound is what the proof uses, and it is the hypothesis that cannot be relaxed by this argument: a rise bounded only along a subsequence leaves the intervening steps free to jump the window. Without a scale restriction on the moduli, Proposition 14.6 gives an unbounded coprime walk with rises 𝑜(log⁡log⁡𝑢𝑛)o(log⁡log⁡un). The same forbidden-block crossing, under a two-sided bound on the error, appears in the proof of Bado’s Theorem 5.1 , posted in September 2026.

The moduli are indexed by the same set as the sequence, and the 𝑖ith of them is asked to divide no value 𝑢𝑡ut with 𝑡 >𝑖t>i; nothing at all is asked of it at or before its own index. That asymmetry is what makes the hypothesis available in the application below, where 𝑚𝑖mi is the 𝑖ith multiplier and only the later numerators are known to be coprime to it.

The barrier applies to the problem because a reduced exact tail already carries pairwise coprime moduli. Call (𝑢,𝑣)(u,v) a reduced exact tail with multipliers 𝑎a when gcd(𝑢𝑛,𝑣𝑛) =1gcd(un,vn)=1,

𝑢𝑛+1+𝑣𝑛=𝑎𝑛𝑢𝑛,𝑣𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝑣𝑛.un+1+vn=anun,vn+1=anvn.

Here 𝑢u is the numerator and 𝑣v the denominator: the two recurrences are those of Section 4, with 𝑢u in the role of the tail state 𝐶C and 𝑣v in that of the denominator state 𝐷D, and with coprimality imposed at every index.

Proposition 11.4 (reduced tails are pairwise coprime). In a reduced exact tail, 𝑎𝑛an is coprime to 𝑣𝑛vn; the multipliers at distinct indices are pairwise coprime; and every earlier multiplier is coprime to every later numerator.

These are the step coprimality, the pairwise coprimality, and the whole-modulus avoidance. Feeding them to Theorem 11.3 gives the form used later: there is no reduced exact tail whose numerator tends to infinity with a uniformly bounded upward increment, the reduced bounded-rise exclusion, together with its eventual form, the eventual reduced exclusion.

Example 11.5 (Sylvester’s sequence as a reduced exact tail). Put 𝑢𝑛 =1un=1 and 𝑣𝑛 =𝐷𝑛 =1,2,6,42,1806,…vn=Dn=1,2,6,42,1806,… as in Example 4.2, with multipliers 𝑎𝑛 =𝑣𝑛 +1 =2,3,7,43,1807,…an=vn+1=2,3,7,43,1807,…. Then gcd(𝑢𝑛,𝑣𝑛) =1gcd(un,vn)=1, 𝑢𝑛+1 +𝑣𝑛 =1 +𝑣𝑛 =𝑎𝑛𝑢𝑛un+1+vn=1+vn=anun and 𝑣𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝑣𝑛vn+1=anvn, so this is a reduced exact tail, and Proposition 11.4 returns the classical fact that Sylvester’s numbers are pairwise coprime. Its numerator is constant, so it satisfies every hypothesis of the exclusion just stated except divergence; since the tail exists, that hypothesis cannot be dropped.

An arbitrary orbit of Section 4 need not be reduced, so one more step is needed before the barrier can be applied to it: the common factor must stop changing. We call a set of indices cofinal when it is infinite, and say that a property holds cofinally when the set of indices at which it holds is cofinal. The step below is the only one connecting the orbit of Section 4 to the reduced tails of Proposition 11.4, and it is where the cofinal boundedness in the proof of Theorem 12.1 is used.

Proposition 11.6 (the tail gcd stabilises). Let (𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)(a,D,C) be an exact natural orbit, that is, a triple of ℕN-valued sequences with 𝐶𝑛+1 +𝐷𝑛 =𝑎𝑛𝐶𝑛Cn+1+Dn=anCn and 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛Dn+1=anDn, whose centred state 𝐸𝑛 =ctr⁡(𝑎𝑛,𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛)En=ctr⁡(an,Dn,Cn) is negative cofinally, with magnitudes bounded along that cofinal set. Then gcd(𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛)gcd(Cn,Dn) is eventually constant, and beyond that index the orbit divided by the stable gcd is a reduced exact tail.

Proof. The tail gcd gcd(𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛)gcd(Cn,Dn) divides its successor, the gcd monotonicity, so the tail gcds form a positive divisibility chain. At an index where the centred state is negative the tail gcd is exactly gcd(𝐶𝑛,𝑒𝑛)gcd(Cn,en), the gcd at a negative index, and is therefore at most the magnitude there; so the chain is bounded along the cofinal set of negative indices. A positive divisibility chain whose values are bounded along a cofinal set is eventually constant, the chain stabilisation. Hence cofinally bounded negative magnitudes make the tail gcd stabilise, the gcd stabilisation, and beyond that point dividing by the stable gcd leaves the numerator and denominator coprime, that is, a reduced exact tail. ◻

The stabilisation of the tail gcd is the checked statement cited at the end of the proof; the last clause, that the divided orbit is a reduced exact tail, is exposition and carries no separate label. Boundedness is required only along a cofinal set. That is what the situation gives: the tail gcd is controlled only at the negative indices, and cofinally many of them is all the divisibility chain needs.

Normalised vanishing by itself gives a different, strictly weaker conclusion. For an exact natural orbit with 𝐶𝑛 >0Cn>0, put

𝐺𝑛=gcd(𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛),Γ(𝑁)=#{0≤𝑗<𝑁:𝐺𝑗<𝐺𝑗+1}.Gn=gcd(Cn,Dn),Γ(N)=#{0≤j<N:Gj<Gj+1}.

Proposition 11.7 (normalised vanishing makes strict gcd changes sparse). Let 𝑎,𝐶,𝐷 :ℕ →ℕa,C,D:N→N satisfy 𝐶𝑛+1 +𝐷𝑛 =𝑎𝑛𝐶𝑛Cn+1+Dn=anCn and 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛Dn+1=anDn with 𝐶𝑛 >0Cn>0, and put 𝐸𝑛 =𝐷𝑛 −(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶𝑛En=Dn−(an−1)Cn, 𝐺𝑛 =gcd(𝐶𝑛,𝐷𝑛)Gn=gcd(Cn,Dn) and Γ(𝑁) =#{0 ≤𝑗 <𝑁 :𝐺𝑗 <𝐺𝑗+1}Γ(N)=#{0≤j<N:Gj<Gj+1}. If |𝐸𝑛|/𝐶𝑛 →0|En|/Cn→0, then Γ(𝑁) =𝑜(𝑁)Γ(N)=o(N). Moreover, for every starting bound 𝐵B and block length 𝐿L, some 𝑛 ≥𝐵n≥B satisfies

𝐺𝑛=𝐺𝑛+1=⋯=𝐺𝑛+𝐿.Gn=Gn+1=⋯=Gn+L.

The first assertion is the sublinear strict-growth theorem; the second is the arbitrarily late constant-block theorem. The proof first converts normalised vanishing into subexponential growth of 𝐶𝑛Cn, then charges every strict divisibility increase of 𝐺𝑛Gn against a finite power-of-two budget. Sparse strict changes force long finite gaps between them.

The quantifiers matter. Proposition 11.6 uses cofinally bounded negative magnitudes and yields eventual constancy. Proposition 11.7 uses only normalised vanishing and yields arbitrarily late constant blocks of each prescribed finite length. It does not yield one infinite constant tail, and it does not exclude cofinally unbounded negative excursions.

Excluding a bounded negative part

Assembling the previous section gives Theorem 12.1, the endpoint of the barrier argument. Theorem 13.1 in the next section uses a different finiteness hypothesis, finite normalised negative mass, by which we mean convergence of ∑𝑛( −𝐸𝑛)+/𝐶𝑛∑n(−En)+/Cn, where 𝑥+ =max(𝑥,0)x+=max(x,0). The two hypotheses ask for different quantities to be estimated, and Theorem 13.1 has the broader ambient setting, since it assumes only the state recurrence with 𝐶𝑛 >0Cn>0. On the common class of exact orbits with normalised vanishing each of them is equivalent to eventual vanishing of the error. For a scalar sequence they differ: hypothesis (5) below holds for a constant negative part −𝑏−b, which gives 𝐶𝑛 ∼𝑏𝑛Cn∼bn and a divergent normalised mass, and such a sequence is excluded as an orbit by Theorem 9.2. The hypotheses of Theorem 12.1 are listed in full to distinguish the abstract arithmetic implication from its canonical application. Normalised vanishing is derived for the canonical orbit and implies eventual strict centring. The bounded negative part is the extra hypothesis that the unrestricted problem does not supply.

Informally, hypotheses (5) and (6) below pull against each other. By Proposition 4.1, hypothesis (5) caps the rise of the tail state at 𝐵B per step, while hypothesis (6), once the error is nowhere zero, forces the tail state to diverge. Proposition 11.6 makes the orbit reduced, and Theorem 11.3 then converts the tension into a contradiction: an integer sequence tending to infinity with upward steps of size at most 𝐵B cannot remain coprime to the pairwise coprime moduli a reduced tail carries. The complementary case, in which the error is eventually positive, is the descent of Theorem 8.1.

Theorem 12.1 (bounded negative part). Let 𝑎,𝐶,𝐷 :ℕ →ℕa,C,D:N→N and 𝐸 :ℕ →ℤE:N→Z satisfy

Then 𝐸𝑛 =0En=0 for all sufficiently large 𝑛n.

Complements and further questions

The results proved here do not resolve Problem #243. The remaining conditions are stated below without treating an equivalent criterion as a proof.

Each exclusion holds only in its stated regime. Theorems 9.2 and 10.1 exclude the constant and the stated periodic magnitudes on an all-negative tail, and do not exclude those patterns merely along the negative indices of a mixed-sign tail; Theorem 12.1 excludes a bounded negative part under normalised vanishing, and Theorem 13.1 excludes finite normalised negative mass with no normalised-vanishing hypothesis. Together with absorption and descent they fix the profile of any counterexample.

Proposition 14.1 (frontier profile for a counterexample). For the canonical integer state attached to any counterexample to Problem 1.1,

𝐸𝑛≠0eventually,|𝐸𝑛|𝐶𝑛⟶0,En≠0eventually,|En|Cn⟶0,

and

lim sup𝑛→∞𝐸𝑛<0(−𝐸𝑛)=∞,∞∑𝑛=0(−𝐸𝑛)+𝐶𝑛=∞.lim supn→∞En<0(−En)=∞,∑n=0∞(−En)+Cn=∞.

In particular, negative indices occur infinitely often. Thus the remaining regime consists of globally coherent, unbounded negative excursions with divergent normalised negative mass.

Theorem 12.1 excludes a bounded negative part, and Theorem 13.1 excludes finite normalised negative mass. These statements are unchanged by deleting a finite prefix. ◻

Every argument in Sections 9–12 uses a finiteness hypothesis: a fixed set of prime divisors, a fixed period, or a fixed bound on the negative part. Theorem 13.1 uses ∑𝑛𝛿𝑛 <∞∑nδn<∞. Proposition 14.1 records that a counterexample has none of them; it is a frontier statement, not an additional problem equivalent to the original one. Problem 14.2 (unbounded divergent-mass negative excursions). Exclude, or construct, an exact natural orbit (𝑎,𝐷,𝐶)(a,D,C) with 𝑎𝑛 >1an>1 and 𝐶𝑛 >0Cn>0, whose multipliers satisfy lim𝑛𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛 =1limnan+1/an2=1 and whose centred state satisfies normalised vanishing, and which is negative infinitely often with magnitudes unbounded along that cofinal set and

An excursion of this kind has none of the finiteness hypotheses just listed. A proposed construction must be global, and it must supply the growth condition of Problem 1.1 together with a vanishing tail ratio, under which the reciprocal-series realisation makes the orbit the canonical orbit of the rational number 𝐶0/𝐷0C0/D0. Finite admissible prefixes alone do not provide such a construction.

This is the repair-entropy inequality.

The square in (22) is the key point. Exact denominator reduction charges 𝑐2𝑛cn2 to the scale growth, so a repaired family whose LCM is at least 2|𝑅|2|R| satisfies

𝐾𝐿4|𝑅|<(𝐾+1)𝐿.KL4|R|<(K+1)L.

The formal consequence is the independent-repair cardinality bound. It rules out positive-density deletion of independent old moduli inside recoveries with a fixed relative-error budget.

There is also an endpoint that does not mention a chosen modulus family. If 𝐾|𝑒𝑛| <𝑢𝑛K|en|<un eventually for every 𝐾K, then for each fixed 𝐿 >0L>0 there is an 𝑁N such that every recovery 𝑢𝑟 ≤𝑢𝑟+𝐿ur≤ur+L with 𝑟 ≥𝑁r≥N satisfies

Thus a surviving nontrivial reset must have recovery length tending to infinity. Lean checks this as eventual disappearance of fixed-length reset payments. The theorem does not bound a recovery length that varies with 𝑟r, nor does it supply a lower bound for the LCM of the moduli repaired in such an interval. Those are the missing inputs needed to turn (22) into a global contradiction.

𝐷0𝐴𝑛=(𝑎𝑛−1)𝐶𝑛+𝐸𝑛D0An=(an−1)Cn+En

one immediately obtains

gcd(𝐴𝑛,𝑎𝑛−1)∣𝐸𝑛.gcd(An,an−1)∣En.

The checked tail-height estimate and normalised vanishing make |𝐸𝑛||En| subexponential in 𝑛n.

Problem 14.4 (old-factor overlap). In every nonterminal canonical orbit satisfying Problem 1.1, is

lim sup𝑛→∞log⁡gcd(𝐴𝑛,𝑎𝑛−1)𝑛>0?lim supn→∞log⁡gcd(An,an−1)n>0?

Equivalently, do there exist 𝜂 >0η>0 and infinitely many 𝑛n such that gcd(𝐴𝑛,𝑎𝑛 −1) ≥𝑒𝜂𝑛gcd(An,an−1)≥eηn?

A positive answer contradicts the displayed divisibility and the subexponential error budget. Arbitrarily long locally admissible blocks do not answer this question: the gcd uses the complete prefix.

The direct analytic question

Problem 14.5 (summability from rationality). Let (𝑎𝑛)(an) satisfy Problem 1.1, and let (𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛,𝐸𝑛)(Dn,Cn,En) be its canonical integer state. Must

∞∑𝑛=0𝛿𝑛=∞∑𝑛=0(−𝐸𝑛)+𝐶𝑛<∞?∑n=0∞δn=∑n=0∞(−En)+Cn<∞?

An affirmative answer closes Problem #243 by Theorem 13.1. Since 𝛿𝑛 →0δn→0, convergence is equivalently expressible as boundedness of the partial products ∏𝑛<𝑁(1 +𝛿𝑛)∏n<N(1+δn); this is the same criterion in multiplicative form. A negative answer requires a sequence satisfying the full growth and rationality hypotheses. A locally admissible state orbit is insufficient. By Theorem 6.2, it is enough to establish the finiteness of (20) for one decreasing weight with divergent integral and one fixed baseline. This replaces the all-index mass by a discounted series supported only at LCM records.

Remark. One further question is not left open here, since it is answered in [12]: whether normalised vanishing follows from 𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛 →1an+1/an2→1 and rationality. It does. After deleting a finite prefix, Koizumi’s Corollary 3  [12] makes the sequence the pseudo-greedy expansion of its own reciprocal sum and gives 𝜀𝑛 →0εn→0 under exactly the hypotheses of Problem 1.1; rationality is not needed for that step, only summability of ∑1/𝑎𝑛∑1/an. Since 𝜀𝑛 =𝐸𝑛/𝐶𝑛εn=En/Cn under the intended reading of Section 4, this is normalised vanishing. Strict centring comes from the same source and is stronger than what Theorem 12.1 assumes: for a rational reciprocal sum, the range −𝑐𝑛/2 ≤𝑒𝑛 <𝑐𝑛/2−cn/2≤en<cn/2 of his Lemma 4(2)  [12] gives |𝐸𝑛| <𝐶𝑛|En|<Cn at every index, which is stronger than eventual strict centring. The eventual form also follows directly from normalised vanishing with 𝐾 =1K=1. What remains unsupplied is hypothesis (5), the bound on the negative part, which is why the theorem is still conditional.

A barrier extension

Proposition 14.6 (no scale-free small-rise extension). There exist strictly increasing primes 𝑝𝑖pi and a strictly increasing positive integer sequence 𝑢𝑛 →∞un→∞ such that gcd(𝑢𝑛,𝑝𝑖) =1gcd(un,pi)=1 for all 𝑖,𝑛i,n and

𝑢𝑛+1−𝑢𝑛=𝑂(√log⁡log⁡(𝑢𝑛+𝑒𝑒))=𝑜(log⁡log⁡(𝑢𝑛+3)).un+1−un=O(log⁡log⁡(un+ee))=o(log⁡log⁡(un+3)).

Thus the proposed variable-rise barrier is false without a quantitative restriction on the sizes or arrival of the moduli.

Proof. Choose increasing primes 𝑝𝑖 >max{exp⁡(exp⁡((𝑖 +2)2)),2𝑖+3}pi>max{exp⁡(exp⁡((i+2)2)),2i+3}, for 𝑖 ≥0i≥0. Primes of arbitrarily large size suffice; no distribution theorem is used. Then 𝜃 =∑𝑖1/𝑝𝑖 <1/4θ=∑i1/pi<1/4 and 𝑘(𝑧) =#{𝑖 :𝑝𝑖 ≤𝑧} ≤√log⁡log⁡𝑧k(z)=#{i:pi≤z}≤log⁡log⁡z whenever 𝑧z is large. For integer 𝑥x put 𝐿(𝑥) =⌈4√log⁡log⁡(𝑥+𝑒𝑒) +8⌉L(x)=⌈4log⁡log⁡(x+ee)+8⌉. Since 𝐿(𝑥) =𝑜(𝑥)L(x)=o(x), eventually 𝐿(𝑥) >𝑘(𝑥 +𝐿(𝑥))/(1 −𝜃)L(x)>k(x+L(x))/(1−θ). The elementary window bound of Proposition 7.15 leaves an integer in [𝑥,𝑥 +𝐿(𝑥))[x,x+L(x)) divisible by no 𝑝𝑖pi. The set of such integers is therefore unbounded. Enumerate it increasingly as (𝑢𝑛)(un) and apply the same bound with 𝑥 =𝑢𝑛 +1x=un+1 to obtain 𝑢𝑛+1 −𝑢𝑛 ≤𝐿(𝑢𝑛 +1)un+1−un≤L(un+1). For prime moduli nondivisibility is exactly coprimality, proving every claim. The moduli are deliberately much sparser than the scale used in the next theorem. ◻

Theorem 14.7 (the static maximal-gap coefficient). Let 𝑚0 <𝑚1 <⋯m0<m1<⋯ be pairwise coprime integers at least 22 with ℓ(𝑚𝑗) =𝑗 +𝑂(1)ℓ(mj)=j+O(1), where ℓ(𝑥) =log2⁡log2⁡max(4,𝑥)ℓ(x)=log2⁡log2⁡max(4,x). Let 𝜎 =∏𝑗(1 −1/𝑚𝑗) >0σ=∏j(1−1/mj)>0 and enumerate the positive integers divisible by no 𝑚𝑗mj as (𝑢𝑛)(un). Then

lim sup𝑛→∞𝑢𝑛+1−𝑢𝑛ℓ(𝑢𝑛)=𝜎−1.lim supn→∞un+1−unℓ(un)=σ−1.

This is a statement about whole-modulus avoidance. It is not a statement about coprimality to composite 𝑚𝑗mj, or about canonical state orbits.

Proof. Write 𝑘(𝑧) =#{𝑗 :𝑚𝑗 ≤𝑧} =ℓ(𝑧) +𝑂(1)k(z)=#{j:mj≤z}=ℓ(z)+O(1). For a fixed prefix length 𝑇T, set

𝑀𝑇=∏𝑗<𝑇𝑚𝑗,𝜎𝑇=∏𝑗<𝑇(1−1/𝑚𝑗),𝜃𝑇=∑𝑗≥𝑇1/𝑚𝑗.MT=∏j<Tmj,σT=∏j<T(1−1/mj),θT=∑j≥T1/mj.

Here 𝜃𝑇 →0θT→0. By the Chinese remainder theorem, avoiding the first 𝑇T whole moduli selects precisely the fraction 𝜎𝑇σT of the residues modulo 𝑀𝑇MT.

For the upper bound, an integer interval [𝑥,𝑥 +𝐿)[x,x+L) contains at least 𝜎𝑇𝐿 −𝑀𝑇σTL−MT integers avoiding that prefix. The remaining moduli cover at most 𝐿𝜃𝑇 +𝑘(𝑥 +𝐿)LθT+k(x+L) integers. Choose 𝑇T large enough that 𝜎𝑇 >𝜃𝑇σT>θT, and then any 𝑐 >(𝜎𝑇 −𝜃𝑇)−1c>(σT−θT)−1. For 𝐿 =⌈𝑐ℓ(𝑥)⌉L=⌈cℓ(x)⌉, the number left is positive for all sufficiently large 𝑥x, since 𝑘(𝑥 +𝐿) =ℓ(𝑥) +𝑂(1)k(x+L)=ℓ(x)+O(1). Thus the set being enumerated is unbounded, and every sufficiently late such interval meets it. Applying this at 𝑥 =𝑢𝑛 +1x=un+1 gives

lim sup𝑛𝑢𝑛+1−𝑢𝑛ℓ(𝑢𝑛)≤(𝜎𝑇−𝜃𝑇)−1.lim supnun+1−unℓ(un)≤(σT−θT)−1.

Letting 𝑇 →∞T→∞ gives the upper bound 𝜎−1σ−1.

For the lower bound, fix 𝑇T and let the integer length 𝐿L tend to infinity. Among the offsets 0 ≤𝑗 <𝐿0≤j<L, precisely 𝐾𝐿 =𝜎𝑇𝐿 +𝑂(𝑀𝑇)KL=σTL+O(MT) avoid the first 𝑇T moduli. Assign to these offsets distinct moduli 𝑚𝑇,…,𝑚𝑇+𝐾𝐿−1mT,…,mT+KL−1. Solve simultaneously 𝑥 ≡0(mod𝑀𝑇)x≡0(modMT) and 𝑥 ≡ −𝑗x≡−j modulo the modulus assigned to 𝑗j. Put 𝑄𝐿 =∏𝑖<𝑇+𝐾𝐿𝑚𝑖QL=∏i<T+KLmi and choose this solution in [𝑄𝐿,2𝑄𝐿)[QL,2QL). Every integer of [𝑥,𝑥 +𝐿)[x,x+L) is then divisible by a modulus: either an old one or its assigned new one. Let 𝑢u be the greatest admissible integer below 𝑥x; its successor is at least 𝑥 +𝐿x+L, so the gap is at least 𝐿L. The scale assumption gives

ℓ(2𝑄𝐿)≤𝑇+𝐾𝐿+𝑂(1),ℓ(2QL)≤T+KL+O(1),

because log2⁡𝑚𝑖 =2𝑖+𝑂(1)log2⁡mi=2i+O(1) and these upper bounds sum geometrically. Since 𝑢 <2𝑄𝐿u<2QL, the ratio for this gap is at least 𝐿/(𝑇 +𝐾𝐿 +𝑂(1))L/(T+KL+O(1)), tending to 𝜎−1𝑇σT−1. These 𝑢u tend to infinity: 𝑥 ≥𝑄𝐿 →∞x≥QL→∞ and admissible integers are unbounded. Hence the limsup is at least 𝜎−1𝑇σT−1 for every 𝑇T. Let 𝑇 →∞T→∞ to finish. ◻

For the Fermat moduli 𝑚𝑗 =22𝑗 +1mj=22j+1, pairwise coprimality and the finite-product identity

𝑁∏𝑗=0(1−122𝑗+1)=22𝑁+1−122𝑁+1−1∏j=0N(1−122j+1)=22N+1−122N+1−1

give 𝜎 =1/2σ=1/2, so the coefficient is exactly 22. The two results above answer the auxiliary questions in the previous draft by ordinary proofs. Neither constructs the positive integer multipliers, integral transports, normalised error or reciprocal-tail realisation required for an example in Problem #243. In particular the static density 𝜎σ must not be substituted for the canonical prefix quantity 𝜑(𝑣𝑇)/𝑣𝑇φ(vT)/vT without a separate argument.

Formalisation targets

Erdős–Straus.

Formalise Theorem 3 of [1], with its prefix-LCM quotient and correctly indexed growth factor, under the published analytic hypotheses.

Duverney.

Formalise Corollary 3.2 of [2], including its signed numerators and its stated convergence hypothesis for the signed defect series, and then recover the all-positive specialisation used here. These are useful verification projects, but neither is an additional open mathematical problem.

Guide to the formal sources

The principal state theorem is in ReciprocalTailRigidity.lean, the scalar finite-mass theorem in SparseResetRecovery.lean, and the entropy inequalities in RepairEntropy.lean. The canonical analytic transfers are separate checked declarations in PaperCompleteR7; their existence must not be inferred from, or denied on the basis of, the abstract state module alone. The periodic exclusion assumes 𝑒𝑛 <𝑎𝑛en<an. The bounded-negative state declaration lists strict centring and normalised vanishing as hypotheses; the latter implies the former eventually by taking 𝐾 =1K=1. Sections 3 and 12 identify the canonical bridge.

A factorial residue reduction for forced orbits

In the case 𝑚 =𝑐 =1m=c=1 of Section 9, where the shape equation (5.1) reads 𝐷𝑛 +1 =(𝑎𝑛 −1)(𝑛 +1)Dn+1=(an−1)(n+1), each multiplier is determined by its predecessor; we call such an orbit forced. At index 𝑛n the numerator of the next multiplier is

num⁡(𝑛,𝑎)=(𝑛+1)𝑎2−(𝑛+2)𝑎+(𝑛+3),num⁡(n,a)=(n+1)a2−(n+2)a+(n+3),

the forced numerator, and the divisor is 𝑛 +2n+2. The orbit survives a step when that division is exact, giving a survival predicate, the survival predicate. Example 9.1 is the forced orbit from 𝑎 =3a=3 read this way: num⁡(0,3) =6num⁡(0,3)=6 is divisible by 22 and gives 𝑎1 =3a1=3, while num⁡(1,3) =13num⁡(1,3)=13 is not divisible by 33, so the orbit stops there. Deciding survival by iteration is expensive because the orbit grows doubly exponentially, and it is unnecessary: survival over a finite horizon depends on the initial value only through a factorial residue. Computing a pseudo-greedy orbit through residues modulo a shrinking product modulus is Koizumi’s method [12]; for the forced numerator that product is a factorial.

Theorem B.1 (factorial residue reduction). For all ℎh and all integers 𝑎 ≡𝑏(mod(ℎ +1)!)a≡b(mod(h+1)!), the orbit from 𝑎a survives ℎh forced updates exactly when the orbit from 𝑏b does.

Proof. Let 𝑀(0,𝑖) =1M(0,i)=1 and 𝑀(ℎ +1,𝑖) =(𝑖 +2)𝑀(ℎ,𝑖 +1)M(h+1,i)=(i+2)M(h,i+1), an ascending factorial with 𝑀(ℎ,0) =(ℎ +1)!M(h,0)=(h+1)!. The numerator is a polynomial with integer coefficients, so congruences transfer; reducing the modulus gives divisibility by 𝑖 +2i+2 for one exactly when for the other, and cancelling that common factor from both values and modulus leaves the inductive hypothesis at 𝑀(ℎ,𝑖 +1)M(h,i+1). ◻

Formalised as the factorial residue reduction, over the shrinking-modulus transport, the polynomial congruence, and the exact-division cancellation; the modulus identifications are the ascending-factorial form and the factorial value at the initial index.

At ℎ =1h=1 the modulus is 2! =22!=2, and surviving one update means 2 ∣𝑎2 −2𝑎 +32∣a2−2a+3, which holds exactly for odd 𝑎a: for instance num⁡(0,3) =6num⁡(0,3)=6 but num⁡(0,4) =11num⁡(0,4)=11. So one step of survival is decided by the parity of 𝑎a alone, which is Theorem B.1 at its smallest nontrivial horizon.

The supplied research record reports a search over initial states below 50005000 that produced forced prefixes of length 1717 and no longer. That historical computation was not rerun in this review; Theorem 9.2 now excludes the constant-negative case outright, for every seed and at every scale. The reduction is retained because it is exact, and because the shrinking-modulus technique transfers to any forced orbit whose step is a polynomial division.

Result map and proof dependencies

The following map is for mathematical navigation, not a catalogue of every registered declaration. A checked component does not confer that status on an assembled ordinary theorem.

Bounded defect.

Canonical rational tail and normalised vanishing ⟶⟶ eventual absorption; cofinally bounded negative values ⟶⟶ stable gcd; reduced tail plus bounded rise ⟶⟶ CRT contradiction. The state endpoint and the identified canonical R7 transfer have supplied main-repository build evidence. The extra bounded-defect assumption is not deduced from the problem.

Finite negative mass.

𝐶𝑛+1 ≤𝐶𝑛(1 +( −𝐸𝑛)+/𝐶𝑛)Cn+1≤Cn(1+(−En)+/Cn) and summability ⟶⟶ bounded integer height ⟶⟶ finitely many rises and eventual constancy. This scalar result needs no normalised vanishing. Its scalar and exact-orbit endpoints are among the cited main-repository declarations; the separately linked R8 canonical formulation is outside that receipt.

Weighted records and protected epochs.

LCM records give weighted first crossings; primitive prime-power persistence gives protected epochs. The canonical odd-power supply and the assembled energy equivalence are proved ordinarily in this revision. Separate-release integer lemmas and main-repository conditional record declarations retain their own, narrower evidence boundaries.

Cubic rate.

The quantitative tail comparison and Gamma-ratio estimate ⟶⟶ integer cubic extraction; transport congruences and Chebotarëv ⟶⟶ a square in the cubic field; trace classification ⟶⟶ two scales, each obstructed modulo seven. The displayed assembly is an ordinary proof. Finite checks and component sources are supporting evidence, not a formalised cubic-rate endpoint.

Static barriers.

Sparse primes disprove a scale-free small-rise extension. At the specified double-exponential modulus scale, prefix density and CRT give the exact whole-modulus maximal-gap coefficient. Both are ordinary auxiliary results, without a canonical reciprocal-tail realisation.

What remains.

The unrestricted problem would require an additional global estimate, such as the stated mass or record budget, or a contradiction to the full nonterminal profile. None of the static examples or local identities supplies one. The more detailed source registry and inherited declaration catalogue remain in the research package rather than being repeated here.
